reasons: No test is visible in this file.
The money helper is exported but not used in this file, so its behaviour is untested here.
Sorting depends on the machine's locale, which could give different orders on different computers.

terms.meaning: one agreed standard way of writing a value so that equal things look identical
a plain text format for storing structured data
the language and regional rules a computer uses to compare and sort text
a comparison that finds what changed between two versions

sections.name: canonicalizeValue
sections.title: Main normalizing entry point
sections.what: Takes any value and returns a cleaned version. Text is tidied, objects and lists are handled by their own helpers, and simple numbers and flags pass through unchanged.
sections.why: Gives every caller one place to clean data of any shape.
sections.watch_out: Values of unusual types are returned untouched, so they may still differ between versions.

sections.name: normalizeWhitespace
sections.title: Collapsing spaces in text
sections.what: Replaces runs of any whitespace, including tabs and line breaks, with a single space and removes the spaces at each end.
sections.why: Stops text that differs only in spacing from looking changed.
sections.watch_out: Line breaks inside a text value are lost, which matters if the text is meant to keep its layout.

sections.name: normalizeMoney
sections.title: Formatting money to two decimals
sections.what: Turns a number or a numeric text into text with exactly two decimal places, or nothing if the value is missing or not a number.
sections.why: Keeps money values written the same way, so 5 and 5.00 compare equal.
sections.watch_out: The rounding comes from the standard number formatter, so very large or unusual values may not be handled as expected.

sections.name: canonicalizeArray
sections.title: Sorting lists of objects
sections.what: Cleans each item in a list, then, when the items are objects, sorts them by a chosen text field. Lists of plain values keep their order.
sections.why: Lists such as people, components or terms can come back in a different order, and sorting them makes the comparison fair.
sections.watch_out: A list whose order actually means something, such as steps in a sequence, will be reordered if its items have a name-like field.

sections.name: determineSortKey
sections.title: Choosing the sort key
sections.what: Picks the text field used for sorting an object list. It checks a preferred list of names first, such as name, role, id and title. If none exist, it uses the first text field in alphabetical order.
sections.why: Gives a stable choice of sort field for records of different kinds.
sections.watch_out: The fallback depends on alphabetical key order, so adding a new field can change which field is used for sorting.

sections.name: canonicalizeObject
sections.title: Sorting object keys
sections.what: Cleans each value in an object and rebuilds the object with its keys in alphabetical order.
sections.why: Two objects with the same contents then produce the same text, whatever order their keys were added in.
sections.watch_out: Only the keys are sorted, so the meaning of the object is not changed, but any code that relies on insertion order will see a different order.

sections.name: canonicalizeForDiff
sections.title: Producing a comparable text form
sections.what: Cleans a value and turns it into a JSON text string. This string is what gets compared when checking whether a record has changed.
sections.why: A single text form makes it easy to say whether two versions are the same.
sections.watch_out: JSON text cannot hold some values, such as undefined inside a list, so those are dropped or changed in the text.

summary: Tidies a value so that two copies with the same meaning produce the same text, which lets the app detect real changes between versions of a record.
purpose: Makes comparisons between old and new data reliable by removing differences in spacing, key order and list order.
why: Likely reason: without a fixed form, the same record could look changed just because its keys were written in a different order.
how: It walks through the value. Text has its spaces collapsed and trimmed. Objects get their keys sorted. Lists are cleaned item by item, then sorted by a name-like field when the items are objects. The final form is turned into a JSON string for comparison.
inputs: Any value: text, a number, a true or false flag, a list, an object, null or nothing.
outputs: A cleaned value of the same general kind, or for the diff helper, a single text string. The money helper returns text with two decimals, or nothing if the input is missing or not a number.
risks: Sorting lists changes their order, which is wrong for lists where order matters. Sorting uses the locale's text rules, which can differ between computers.
debug: If two equal records look different, compare their canonical text output. If a list seems to change order, check whether its first item has a name-like field, since that is what triggers sorting.
